From 1965 to 1977 this Ukrainian-born official served as Chairman of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet — effectively the Soviet head of state. Who was he?
A brigadier general who seized power in a 1989 coup and ruled Sudan under various titles until a 2019 coup toppled him, after which he was jailed and convicted of corruption — who is he?
Omar al-Bashir: President of Sudan from 1989 to 2019.
An American civil servant, diplomat and artist, he's remembered chiefly as the husband of a celebrated TV chef and cookbook author — who is he?
Named the first viceroy of Italian East Africa, this general commanded Italian forces in both world wars and became Prime Minister after Fascism fell — who was he?

Beginning in 230 BC, King Ying Zheng launched a decade of campaigns swallowing six rival states one by one — Han, Zhao, Yan, Wei, Chu and Qi — ending the Warring States period in 221 BC. What were these campaigns?
Qin's wars of unification: Qin campaigns to conquer all of China (230–221 BC)
Historians use this name for the wave of anticlerical violence — killings and church arson — carried out by leftist groups during the Spanish Civil War; what's it called?
Golden age of arcade video games
Red Terror (Spain): Assassinations during the Spanish Civil War.
As Colombia's Minister of Justice, he cracked down on cocaine traffickers until he was assassinated on the orders of a notorious drug baron in 1984 — who was he?
Rodrigo Lara Bonilla: Colombian lawyer and politician (1946-1984)

Using the alias Saitani Umetarō while hunted by shogunate forces, this low-ranking samurai from Tosa negotiated the alliance between rival domains that helped topple the Tokugawa Shogunate — who was he?
Sakamoto Ryōma: Japanese samurai and politician (1836–1867)

This wave of mass production, standardization, and rapid scientific discovery, sometimes dubbed the Technological era, is generally dated between 1870 and the outbreak of World War I in 1914. What period was this?
Second Industrial Revolution: 1870–1914 electrical and chemical era.
A writer who governed Tokyo from 1999 to 2012, this prominent ultranationalist was widely criticized for xenophobic and racist remarks against Chinese and Koreans in Japan — who was he?
Across religions this immortal, immaterial essence goes by many names — atman in Hinduism, jiva in Jainism, ruh in Islam — but what's its common English term?
Soul: In religion and philosophy, immaterial essence of a living being.
Known at home as the 'Great Power Era,' this 17th-century Baltic dominion began with Gustavus Adolphus's ascension in 1611 and collapsed after the Great Northern War in 1721 — which power?
Swedish Empire: Historical period in the history of Sweden (1611–1721)

Known in Hebrew as the Shoah, this World War II genocide killed roughly six million people — about two-thirds of Europe's Jewish population — through mass shootings and gas chambers at camps like Auschwitz-Birkenau. What is it?
The Holocaust: Genocide of European Jews by Nazi Germany.
This British Labour politician sat in the Commons for 47 of 51 years and later presided over the Stop the War Coalition — though for a stretch he was known as The Viscount Stansgate — who is he?
Tony Benn: British politician and activist (1925–2014)
This Germanic people allied with Rome during the Marcomannic Wars before later conquering and ruling Roman North Africa until 534 CE — who were they?
Serving under Jimmy Carter, this Minnesota senator became the 42nd U.S. vice president and the Democratic Party's presidential nominee in 1984 — who is he?
Walter Mondale: Vice President of the United States from 1977 to 1981.

Dubbed 'the Great Commoner' and 'the Boy Orator' for his faith in ordinary people and his thundering rhetoric, this Nebraskan was the Democrats' presidential nominee three times — in 1896, 1900, and 1908. Who was he?
This retired Turkish general served as the 30th Chief of the General Staff of the Turkish Armed Forces before becoming Minister of National Defense — who is he?
Yaşar Güler: Turkish general and politician (born 1954)
Son of Edward the Elder, this ruler is regarded by modern historians as the first King of England; he never married and was succeeded by his half-brother Edmund — who is he?
Æthelstan: King of the English from 927 to 939.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Georges Dumézil (born 1898) is the earliest of the four. Dumézil is well known for his formulation of the trifunctional hypothesis on Proto-Indo-European mythology and society.
Which of these four is the eldest?
Henry Vaughan (born 1621) is the earliest of the four. Henry Vaughan (1621 – 23 April 1695) was a Welsh metaphysical poet, author and translator writing in English, and a medical physician.
Which of these four began earliest?
Python (programming language) (founded 1991) is the earliest of the four. Python supports multiple programming paradigms but with an emphasis on object-oriented programming and dynamic typing.
Which of these four dates back furthest?

Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four. Fortran (formerly FORTRAN) is a third-generation, compiled, imperative programming language designed for numeric computation and scientific computing.
Pick the astronomer from these four.
Williamina Fleming is an astronomer. Williamina Paton Stevens Fleming (15 May 1857 – 21 May 1911) was a Scottish astronomer.
Who among these is a mathematician?
Carl Friedrich Gauss is a mathematician. Gauss was director of the Göttingen Observatory in Germany and professor of astronomy from 1807 until his death in 1855.
What is the atomic number of Rutherfordium?
Rutherfordium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Rf and atomic number 104.
What is the atomic number of Selenium?
Selenium is a chemical element; it has symbol Se and atomic number 34.
In what year was Buzz Aldrin born?
Buzz Aldrin ( AWL-drin; born Edwin Eugene Aldrin Jr.; January 20, 1930) is an American former astronaut, aeronautical engineer, and fighter pilot.
In what year was Christine Lagarde born?
Christine Lagarde: Lagarde had also served in the Government of France, most prominently as Minister of the Economy, Finance and Industry from 2007 until 2011.
In what year was Ernest Rutherford born?
Ernest Rutherford: Together with Thomas Royds, Rutherford is credited with proving that alpha radiation is composed of helium nuclei.
In what year did Arthur Conan Doyle die?
Arthur Conan Doyle: Sir Arthur Ignatius Conan Doyle (22 May 1859 – 7 July 1930) was a British writer and physician.
In what year did Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz die?
Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz: Leibniz, along with René Descartes and Baruch Spinoza, was one of the three influential early modern rationalists.
In what year was Oxygen discovered?
Oxygen is a chemical element; it has the symbol O and its atomic number is 8.
Potassium chloride: Pfizer. Potassium chloride (KCl, or potassium salt) is a metal halide salt composed of potassium and chlorine.
Rendang: Indonesia. It refers to both a cooking method of frying and the dish cooked in that way.
Who is credited with discovering Musca?
Musca: Petrus Plancius. Musca (Latin for 'the fly') is a small constellation in the deep southern sky.
Who is credited with discovering Testosterone?
Testosterone: János Freud. Testosterone is the primary male sex hormone and androgen in males.
Who is credited with discovering Cyanoacrylate?
Cyanoacrylate: Harry Coover. The cyanoacrylate group in the monomer rapidly polymerizes in the presence of water to form long, strong chains.
Who is credited with discovering Rubidium?
Rubidium: Robert Bunsen. Rubidium is a chemical element; it has symbol Rb and atomic number 37.
This Swiss chemist discovered the structure of chitin in 1929 and decades later authored a memoir titled 'LSD: My Problem Child' — who was he?
Albert Hofmann (11 January 1906 - 29 April 2008) was a Swiss chemist known for being the first to synthesize, ingest, and learn of the psychedelic effects of lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD).
Whether from too few red blood cells or faulty hemoglobin, this disorder leaves the blood less able to carry oxygen — often felt as quiet tiredness long before any paleness shows — what is it?
Anemia (also spelt anaemia in British English) is a blood disorder in which the blood has a reduced ability to carry oxygen.

A German former computer repair technician, this man received international attention after murdering and cannibalizing a voluntary victim he had found over the Internet in March 2001, and was ultimately convicted of murder in a 2006 retrial — who is he?

Armin Meiwes (born 1 December 1961) is a German former computer repair technician who received international attention for murdering and cannibalising Bernd Brandes, whom he had found via the Internet as a voluntary victim, in March 2001.
Only eight species of this stocky-legged, shaggy, short-tailed carnivoran survive, ranging across North and South America and Eurasia — what mammal is it?
Bear are carnivoran mammals of the family Ursidae.
A child prodigy who wrote a treatise on conic sections at 16, which Frenchman later traded letters with Fermat on probability and built early calculating machines?
Blaise Pascal (19 June 1623 - 19 August 1662) was a French mathematician, physicist, inventor, philosopher, and Catholic writer.
This small leafy vegetable, a cultivar of cabbage grown for its edible buds, shares its name with a European capital — what is it?
Brussels sprout is a member of the Gemmifera cultivar group of cabbages (Brassica oleracea), grown for its edible buds.

Honored twice by the American Psychological Association — in 1956 for scientific contributions and 1972 for professional ones — this psychologist championed a person-centered approach to therapy — who is he?
Carl Rogers (January 8, 1902 - February 4, 1987) was an American psychologist who was one of the founders of humanistic psychology and was known especially for his person-centered psychotherapy.

This compound is a yellowish-green gas above 11°C, a reddish-brown liquid when cooler, and bright orange crystals when very cold — usually handled in solution as a bleach and disinfectant. What is it?

Chlorine dioxide is a chemical compound with the formula ClO2 that exists as yellowish-green gas above 11 C (52 F), a reddish-brown liquid between 11 and 59 C (52 and 74 F), and as bright orange crystals below 59 C (74 F).
What's the scientific family name for the group of birds that includes both doves and pigeons — stout-bodied birds with small heads and no formal distinction between the two common names?
Columbidae is a bird family consisting of doves and pigeons.
Mostly aquatic mandibulate arthropods, this group spans shrimp, crayfish, copepods, and barnacles — and modern science now files insects in alongside them — what are they?
Crustacean (from Latin word "crustacea" meaning: "those with shells" or "crusted ones") are mandibulate arthropods that are traditionally a part of the paraphyletic subphylum Crustacea.
A colorless organosulfur compound known as the most widely used commercial sulfoxide, an important polar solvent. It leaves a distinctive taste when absorbed through the skin. What is it?
Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) is an organosulfur compound with the formula (CH3)2S=O.
Sometimes occurring spontaneously during sleep as a nocturnal emission, this process involves the discharge of semen through the urethra — what is it called?
Ejaculation is the discharge of semen (the ejaculate; normally containing sperm) from the penis through the urethra.
From abortion to animal welfare to business practices, the 'applied' branch of this philosophical study tackles real-world moral problems. What is it?
Ethics is the philosophical study of moral phenomena. Its main branches include normative ethics, applied ethics, and metaethics.
This common long-term inflammatory airway disease causes wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath that can flare into sudden attacks triggered by allergens or pollen. What condition is it?
Flamingo are a type of wading bird in the family Phoenicopteridae, which is the only extant family in the order Phoenicopteriformes.
Its name literally means 'Earth writing,' and it explores not just where things are but how they changed and came to be across the planet — what field is it?
Geography (from Ancient Greek geographia; combining ge 'Earth' and graphein 'write', lit. 'Earth writing') is the study of the lands, features, inhabitants, and phenomena of planet Earth.

Native to the Amazon basin, this climbing plant's coffee-bean-sized seeds can contain up to 6% caffeine — roughly double the concentration found in green coffee beans — and flavor a popular Brazilian soft drink. Name the plant?
Guarana (from the Portuguese guaran; Paullinia cupana, syns.

This colorless, nearly odorless organic compound is a straight-chain alkane with six carbon atoms, widely used as a cheap, largely unreactive solvent and found in small amounts in modern gasoline blends — what is it?
Hexane is an organic compound, a straight-chain alkane with six carbon atoms and the molecular formula C6H14.
Marked by shivering and confusion in mild cases and hallucinations or paradoxical undressing in severe cases, this condition is defined as a body core temperature below 35°C (95°F) — name it?
Hypothermia is defined as a body core temperature below 35.0 C (95.0 F) in humans.
A pioneer of radio microwave optics who also wrote science fiction and has a lunar crater named for him, this Indian polymath founded Asia's first interdisciplinary research institute — who was he?
Jagadish Chandra Bose (30 November 1858 - 23 November 1937) was an Indian polymath with interests in biology, physics and writing science fiction.
Named after a 19th-century English physicist, this SI unit of energy equals the work done when a one-newton force moves an object one metre in the direction of that force — name the unit?
Joule (JOOL, or JOWL; symbol: J) is the unit of energy in the International System of Units (SI).
This broadly distributed genus of spiders is informally grouped under a nickname referencing marital loss, encompassing both black and brown members — what is its scientific name?
Latrodectus is a broadly distributed genus of spiders informally called the widow spiders, with several species that are commonly known as the true widows.
Known mainly from fossils in Peru's Pisco Formation, this Miocene-era macroraptorial sperm whale takes its name from a biblical sea monster — what is it called?
Livyatan is an extinct genus of highly predatory macroraptorial sperm whale, containing one known species: L. melvillei.
Its Spanish name translates to 'little apple of death' — this tropical tree's apple-like fruit and toxic milky sap make it one of the most poisonous trees on Earth — which tree?
Manchineel (Hippomane mancinella), also known as the tree of death, is a species of flowering plant in the spurge family (Euphorbiaceae).
Home to a relativistic plasma jet stretching nearly 5,000 light-years from its core, this giant elliptical galaxy sits in the constellation Virgo — which galaxy is it?
Messier 87 (also known as Virgo A or NGC 4486, generally abbreviated to M87) is a supergiant elliptical galaxy in the constellation Virgo that contains several trillion stars.
Its English name passed from Greek to Latin to Portuguese before landing in English in the early 1600s — which family of roughly 200 marine fish species boasts 16 genera?
Moray eel are a family of eels whose members are found worldwide.
Composed of a renal corpuscle and a renal tubule, this microscopic structural and functional unit of the kidney numbers between 1 and 1.5 million per healthy adult kidney — name it?

Nephron is the minute or microscopic structural and functional unit of the kidney. The renal corpuscle consists of a tuft of capillaries called a glomerulus and a cup-shaped structure called Bowman's capsule.
This Persian polymath and poet was the first to provide a general geometric solution to all third-degree polynomial equations, using the intersection of conic sections. Who is he?
Omar Khayyam (1048-1131) was a Persian poet and polymath, known for his contributions to mathematics, astronomy, philosophy, and Persian literature.
This galliform game bird, native to Europe, Asia, and Africa, was once lumped in with pheasants and quail, but DNA suggests it isn't one distinct group at all — which bird is it?
Partridge is a medium-sized galliform bird in any of several genera, with a wide native distribution throughout parts of Europe, Asia and Africa.
Colorless in acid and a vivid pink in base, which phthalein dye is the chemist's go-to indicator for acid-base titrations?
Phenolphthalein (feh-NOL(F)-th-leen) is a chemical compound with the formula C20H14O4 and is often written as "HIn", "HPh", "phph" or simply "Ph" in shorthand notation.

This academic field studies systems of governance and power, favoring descriptive and empirical analysis of behavior and institutions over the value judgments used in philosophy about the state — name the discipline?
Political science (sometimes abbreviated as poli sci) is a field which aims to study the scientific aspect of politics.

Named early in the history of microbiology for its widespread presence in water and plant seeds, which genus of gram-negative bacteria includes an opportunistic human pathogen infamous in hospitals as well as plant and soil-dwelling species?
Pseudomonas is a genus of gram-negative bacteria belonging to the family Pseudomonadaceae in the class Gammaproteobacteria.
First flown in 1955 as a nuclear-strike follow-on to the Mach 1 Super Sabre, this fighter-bomber earned the nickname 'Thud' and flew most early Vietnam War strike missions — which aircraft?
Republic F-105 Thunderchief is an American fighter-bomber that served with the United States Air Force from 1958 to 1984.

Known from complete specimens found in Bolivia, this extinct armored jawless fish from the Ordovician period resembled a slender tadpole with eyes set like car headlamps on its oversized head — what is it?
Sacabambaspis is an extinct genus of armored jawless fish which lived in the Ordovician period.
This Russian politician has served as mayor of Moscow since 2010, after earlier stints as a regional governor, head of the presidential administration, and deputy prime minister — who is he?
Sergey Sobyanin (born 21 June 1958) is a Russian politician, serving as the 3rd mayor of Moscow since 21 October 2010.
Mostly made from potato starch but also lurking in apples and berries, this slowly-metabolized sugar alcohol is an isomer of mannitol, differing only by one hydroxyl group's orientation — what is it?
Sorbitol is a sugar alcohol with a sweet taste which the human body metabolizes slowly.
This small nocturnal marsupial sails between trees on membranes stretched from wrist to ankle, and its Latin name translates as 'short-headed rope-dancer' — what animal is it?
Sugar glider (Petaurus breviceps) is a small, omnivorous, arboreal, and nocturnal gliding possum.

This family of marine and freshwater fish can inflate themselves dramatically, revealing thin spines that stay hidden against their skin until they puff up — unlike their spinier, porcupine-like relatives — name this fish family?
Tetraodontidae is a family of marine and freshwater fish in the order Tetraodontiformes.

Stretching from the base of the skull down to the lower back and out to each shoulder blade, this large paired muscle supports the arm and moves the scapula in three distinct ways — what's the muscle?
Trapezius is a large paired trapezoid-shaped surface muscle that extends longitudinally from the occipital bone to the lower thoracic vertebrae of the spine and laterally to the spine of the scapula.

Named after an 18th-century Italian physicist and first published in 1797, this phenomenon explains why fluid pressure drops as it speeds up through a narrower pipe section — powering wine aerators and vacuum ejectors. What is it called?
Venturi effect is the reduction in fluid pressure that results when a moving fluid speeds up as it is funneled from one section of a pipe to another, smaller section.
Chairman of the Polish People's Party since 2015 and a former Minister of Labour and Social Affairs, this physician-turned-politician ran for the Polish presidency in 2020 — who is he?
Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (born 10 August 1981) is a Polish physician and politician, who has served as the Deputy Prime Minister of Poland, and Minister of National Defence since 2023.
The simplest alkyne, this colorless gas packs all four of its atoms into one straight line thanks to a carbon-carbon triple bond, and fuels welding torches — which compound is it?
First nominated by Ronald Reagan in 1987 and reappointed every four years until 2006, this soft-spoken economist logged the second-longest tenure ever as chairman of the Federal Reserve — who was he?
Alan Greenspan: American economist and financial advisor (born 1926)
Nicknamed the boto for its rosy pink hue (especially in males), this South American toothed whale is the largest species of its kind found in a freshwater habitat — what is it?
Amazon river dolphin: Species of toothed whale. The position of the Araguaian river dolphin (I. araguaiaensis) within the clade is still unclear.
Named from Greek words for 'curved' and 'vertebra,' this type of arthritis causes long-term inflammation where the spine meets the pelvis — what is it?
Ankylosing spondylitis: Type of arthritis of the spine. Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a type of arthritis from the disease spectrum of axial spondyloarthritis.
The fourth-brightest star in the night sky and the brightest in the northern hemisphere, this aging red giant in Boötes has ballooned to 25 times the Sun's size despite sharing its mass — what is it?
Arcturus: Brightest star in the constellation Boötes. It has the Bayer designation α Boötis, which is Latinized to Alpha Boötis and abbreviated Alpha Boo or α Boo.

Also called the moon jellyfish, this once-thought-cosmopolitan species was split into roughly 28 separate species in the 2020s and is now known to live only in the north Atlantic and off Argentina — which species?
Aurelia aurita: Species of jellyfish. The species now identified as A. aurita is only found in the north Atlantic and in Argentina, and is not dangerous to humans.

This single-engine turboprop trainer, a license-built version of the Swiss Pilatus PC-9, replaced America's Cessna 'Tweet' and Turbo Mentor trainers in the 2010s and flies under the nickname 'Efroni' in Israel — which aircraft?
Beechcraft T-6 Texan II: Single-engine, low-wing tandem-seat turboprop military training aircraft.

Despite its name, this snake is actually grey to dark brown — the name instead describes the dark interior of its mouth, displayed as a threat — which species, the second-longest venomous snake after the king cobra?
Black mamba: Species of venomous snake. The black mamba (Dendroaspis polylepis) is a species of highly venomous snake belonging to the family Elapidae.
Cattle, bison, buffalo, and goat-antelopes like sheep and goats all belong to this family of cloven-hoofed ruminants with over 140 living species — what is it?
Bovidae: Family of mammals belonging to even-toed ungulates.
Historically hardware-dependent in size, ranging anywhere from 1 to 48 bits, this unit of digital information now almost always means eight bits — what's it called?
Byte: Unit of digital information, usually 8 bits.
With the formula H2CO3, this fleeting compound has a lifespan of only about 20 milliseconds at body temperature before converting to water and carbon dioxide — which compound?
Carbonic acid: Chemical compound. The molecule rapidly converts to water and carbon dioxide in the presence of water.
Nicknamed 'no-see-ums' for their tiny 1-3mm size, these biting midges are also among the best-studied pollinators of cocoa plants — what is this fly family called?
Ceratopogonidae: Family of flies commonly known as no see ums, or biting midges.
Usually triggered when a gallstone blocks the cystic duct, this inflammatory condition causes right-upper abdominal pain that radiates to the shoulder — what is it?
Their 'lady' actually refers to the Virgin Mary, and their cheerful red-and-black warning colours tell predators they taste terrible — what is this 6,000-species family of small beetles?
Coccinellidae: Family of beetles. The more than 6,000 described species have a global distribution and are found in a variety of habitats.
First created near Darmstadt in 1996 and named for an astronomer on his 537th anniversary, this synthetic element (number 112) is so volatile it may even be a gas — which element?
Copernicium: Chemical element with atomic number 112 (Cn)
First flown in 1938 and built almost 14,000 strong at a factory in Buffalo, New York, this WWII fighter-bomber was known to British and Soviet pilots as the Tomahawk or Kittyhawk — which aircraft?
Curtiss P-40 Warhawk: American WWII fighter. The Curtiss P-40 Warhawk is an American single-engined, single-seat, all-metal fighter-bomber that first flew in 1938.
Spread by mosquitoes in tropical regions, this virus is often mild but can turn severe with bleeding, plummeting platelet counts, and dangerously low blood pressure — what is it?
Synthesized from L-DOPA in the brain and kidneys, this catecholamine acts as a neurotransmitter and drives a major brain pathway tied to reward and motivation — what is it?
Dopamine: Organic chemical that functions both as a hormone and a neurotransmitter.
Belonging to the order Anguilliformes and comprising roughly 1,000 species, these ray-finned predators transform dramatically from larva to adult and mostly live in salt water — what are they?
This fungal genus growing on rye and other cereals produces alkaloids that cause a poisoning condition in humans and livestock who eat contaminated grain — which group of fungi?
Ergot: Fungi of the genus Claviceps. The most prominent member of this group is Claviceps purpurea (rye ergot fungus).

Its mating has never once been observed in the wild, and its five life stages were once mistaken for five separate species — this critically endangered fish is threatened by dams and overfishing. What is it?
European eel: Species of fish. The five stages of their development were originally thought to be different species.
When fibroblasts overproduce collagen after repeated injury or chronic inflammation, this permanent connective-tissue scarring can impair an organ's normal function — what is it called?
Fibrosis: Excess connective tissue in healing.
Known for wood used in tool handles, electric guitars, and Morgan Motor Company's sports car frames, this tree genus produced nymphs called the Meliae in Greek myth — which genus?
Fraxinus: Genus of plants. The genus is widespread throughout much of Europe, Asia, and North America.
With a siphon that can stretch over three feet and a shell just 6 to 8 inches across, this giant Pacific burrowing clam can live up to 179 years — which creature?
This type of organ produces an organism's sex hormones and gametes — testicles in males, ovaries in females — what is it called?
Gonad: Gland that produces sex cells.
This standard markup language structures web documents using elements delineated by tags, often paired with CSS and JavaScript — what is it?
HTML: Markup language for documents. Hypertext Markup Language (HTML) is the standard markup language for documents designed to be displayed in a web browser.
This natural anticoagulant boosts the activity of antithrombin and is used to prevent clotting during dialysis and in blood test tubes — what medication is it?
Heparin: Anticoagulant. Heparin, also known as unfractionated heparin (UFH), is a medication and naturally occurring glycosaminoglycan.

This American physicist dared to drop the wave-function-collapse postulate, proposing a 'relative state' theory that became the basis of the many-worlds interpretation — largely ignored until quantum decoherence vindicated him. Who is he?
Known as 'the father of modern optics,' this Islamic Golden Age scholar wrote the influential 'Book of Optics' and proved that vision begins in the eye, not by rays leaving it — who is he?
Ibn al-Haytham: Arab physicist, mathematician and astronomer (c. 965 – c. 1040)
Awarded the 1906 Nobel Prize in Physics, this British scientist discovered in 1897 that cathode rays were made of what we now call electrons — who is he?

This American physicist worked with Niels Bohr on nuclear fission and had a gift for coinages — "quantum foam," "wormhole," and the term that popularized "gravitationally collapsed objects." Who was he?
John Archibald Wheeler: American theoretical physicist (1911–2008)
Named from a Tongan and Marquesan word meaning 'bitter,' this pepper-family plant's ground root becomes a ceremonial Pacific Islands drink that numbs the mouth — what is it?
Kava: Species of plant. Kava or kava kava (Piper methysticum: Latin 'pepper' and Latinized Greek 'intoxicating') is a plant in the pepper family, native to the Pacific Islands.
This broadly distributed genus of spiders is informally known as the widow spiders, including the black widow and brown widow — what is it called?
Latrodectus: Genus of spiders. Latrodectus is a broadly distributed genus of spiders informally called the widow spiders, with several species that are commonly known as the true widows.
Creator of both a widely used open-source operating system kernel and the version-control system Git, this engineer won the 2012 Millennium Technology Prize — who is he?
Linus Torvalds: Finnish and American software engineer (born 1969)
Described in the New Testament as a physician, this traditional author of two New Testament books is said to have been martyred by hanging from an olive tree — who is he?
Luke the Evangelist: One of the four traditionally ascribed authors of the canonical gospels.
Also known as sapodilla, this evergreen tree native to Mexico and Central America was carried to the Philippines by Spanish colonizers — which species?
Manilkara zapota: Species of tropical evergreen tree.
Isolated in 1958 from cow pineal glands because it could lighten frog skin, this nighttime brain hormone turned out to be the body's regulator of the sleep-wake cycle — what is it?
Melatonin: Hormone released by the pineal gland.
Often striking one side of the head and sometimes preceded by a sensory 'aura,' this neurological disorder brings nausea and sensitivity to light and sound — what is it?
Migraine: Disorder resulting in recurrent moderate–severe headaches.

Nicknamed the Swiss cheese plant for its perforated leaves, this houseplant native to southern Mexico and Central America produces a fruit that's edible once ripe, despite needle-like calcium oxalate crystals elsewhere in the plant — what is its scientific name?
Monstera deliciosa: Species of plant. Monstera deliciosa, the Swiss cheese plant or split-leaf philodendron, is a species of flowering plant.
Made of the same tough protein as claws, hooves, and horns, this protective plate covers the tip of your fingers and toes — what is it?
Nail (anatomy): Hard keratin protection of digit.
Sold under the brand name Macrobid, this antibacterial drug treats lower urinary tract infections but isn't effective against kidney infections. What is it?
Nitrofurantoin: Antibacterial drug. Nitrofurantoin, sold under the brand name Macrobid among others, is an antibacterial medication of the nitrofuran class.
First described in 1689 by a local naturalist, this aquatic cave-dwelling salamander is the only exclusively cave-dwelling chordate native to Europe — what is it?
Britain, Germany, and Italy jointly built this twin-engine, variable-sweep-wing combat jet through a tri-national consortium, first flying it in 1974 — which aircraft?
Panavia Tornado: Family of multi-role combat aircraft.
This psychiatric paraphilia involves a primary or exclusive sexual attraction to prepubescent children, with diagnostic criteria extending the cutoff age to thirteen — which disorder?
Pedophilia: Sexual attraction to prepubescent children. The DSM requires the arousal pattern must be present for 6 months or longer, while the ICD lacks this requirement.
This branch of linguistics studies how spoken languages organize meaningful sound units — the kind of contrast that separates 'bat' from 'gnat' — what field is it?
Phonology: Study of sound organization in languages.
Its name comes from the Greek for 'making,' and it leans on devices like assonance, alliteration, and metre to evoke meanings beyond the literal — what literary art is this?

Detected by receptors in your muscles, tendons, and joints, this sense tells your brain where your body is in space, working alongside vision and balance to keep you upright and coordinated — what's it called?
Proprioception: Sense of self-movement, force, and body position.
Found in notable amounts in capers, red onions, and kale, this bitter-tasting plant flavonol is a popular ingredient in dietary supplements — what compound?
Quercetin: Chemical compound. It is found in many fruits, vegetables, leaves, seeds, and grains; capers, red onions, and kale are common foods containing appreciable amounts of it.
Often compared to the film in a camera, this innermost, light-sensitive layer of the eye sends signals along the optic nerve to the visual cortex — what is it?
Retina: Part of the eye. The retina (from Latin rete 'net'; pl. retinae or retinas) is the innermost, light-sensitive layer of tissue of the eye.
Discovered in 1973 by Ruth Bishop via electron micrograph images, this fecal-oral pathogen is the leading cause of diarrheal illness in infants worldwide — which pathogen?
Rotavirus: Specific genus of RNA viruses.
